title: Big questions
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: THE ABSTRACT NOUNS ARE A SUFFIX, NOT A VOCABULARY LIST. -tās and -tūdō make an abstract out of an adjective and BOTH ARE FEMININE, without exception: vērus gives vēritās, līber gives lībertās, fortis gives fortitūdō. A learner with forty-nine rungs of adjectives can now make nouns out of all of them, which is the most productive single thing this level teaches — and English has borrowed both endings, so recognition is free and the ENDING is what has to be learned. The suffix decides the gender, not the adjective it came from.

ABSTRACT TALK NEEDS NO NEW CONSTRUCTION AT ALL: quid est plus a -tās noun. L1-M2 taught the question word and L1-M1 the verb, and the abstraction lives entirely in the suffix — so quid est vēritās? is three words the course has had since its second module, and it is the question Pilate asks in the Vulgate.

virtūs IS THE COGNATE TRAP MADE A LESSON. It is vir ('man') plus -tūs, so literally 'manliness' — hence courage, hence excellence of any kind. It does NOT mean 'virtue' in the modern moral sense, and a Roman praising a WOMAN's virtūs was paying a real compliment with a word built out of 'man'. This module states the Roman meaning and the English one side by side and chooses neither, because the drift is the fact worth knowing.

crēdō TAKES TWO CONSTRUCTIONS AND WHAT IS BELIEVED DECIDES WHICH. A PROPOSITION takes the accusative and infinitive — crēdō deōs esse, which is L3-M3's shape on a new verb. A PERSON takes the DATIVE — crēdō tibi, 'I believe you', and crēdō tē is not Latin. L3-M3's putō had only the first, so this is the first verb in the course whose construction depends on what is believed rather than on the verb itself — and S06 has both in one sentence, four words apart.

nēmō IS THE SEVENTH WORD IN THIS COURSE WITH A NEGATIVE INSIDE IT, after L1-M3's nōlō, L2-M9's mālō, L3-M5's negō, L4-M3's nisi, L4-M5's nesciō and L4-M6's nōndum. It is nē plus homō and it takes NO nōn — nēmō nōn scit is a real idiom meaning 'everybody knows', which is the opposite of what a learner will mean. Two negatives in ONE clause cancel; two in TWO clauses do not, which is what S08 is for.

omnīnO AFTER AN ABSOLUTE WORD IS A HEDGE. L4-M5 taught nōn omnīnō as 'not entirely'; nēmō omnīnō scit turns a claim nobody could defend into one somebody might. That is the whole apparatus of abstract talk in the hands of somebody honest — and it costs nothing, because the word has been available since L4-M5.

words.note: 'I believe': crēdō, crēdit. It takes an accusative and infinitive for a BELIEF and a dative for a PERSON — two constructions, one verb.
'You' — the DATIVE, because believing a PERSON takes it. crēdō tibi is 'I believe you' and crēdō tē would be wrong.
'Not', in front of what it denies.
'However', and it comes SECOND in its clause. L3-M3's word.
'I believe': crēdō, crēdit. It takes an accusative and infinitive for a BELIEF and a dative for a PERSON — two constructions, one verb.
'Truth' as the object of the reported clause — vēritās as the subject, vēritātem inside a report. The -tās suffix declines like any noun.
'To be' — sum's infinitive.

sentences.trap: THE SAME VERB TWICE AND TWO DIFFERENT CASES. crēdō tibi is a person and takes the dative; crēdō vēritātem esse is a proposition and takes the accusative with an infinitive. L3-M3's putō had only the second, so this is the first verb in the course whose construction depends on WHAT is believed rather than on the verb itself.

sentences.display: Nēmō crēdit lībertātem magnam nōn esse.
sentences.cue: Nobody believes that freedom is not a great thing.
sentences.literal: nobody he-believes freedom great not to-be

words.note: 'Nobody' — nē plus homō welded together, and the SEVENTH word in this course with a negative inside it. It takes no nōn.
'He believes' — crēdō, crēdit, and here the subject is an indefinite, so the third person.
'Freedom' as the object of the reported clause — lībertās as the subject, lībertātem inside a report.
'Great' in the object shape, agreeing with lībertātem. L2-M3's adjective, moving with its noun into a reported clause.
'Not', and here it denies the INFINITIVE rather than crēdit. Nobody believes that it is NOT great.
'To be' — sum's infinitive.

sentences.trap: Two negatives in one sentence and they do not cancel, because they belong to different clauses. nēmō negates the believing and nōn negates the being great — so the sentence means everybody thinks freedom IS great, which is what you get by denying a denial across a clause boundary rather than inside one.
